traveler: William Jefferson Clinton (born William Jefferson Blythe III)
title: From the Rose Garden Handshake to the Ground Set Aside: Hope, the White House, and the Flight Logs
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Hope, Hot Springs, and the Rose Garden

stops.name: Hope, Arkansas: the birth of William Jefferson Blythe III
stops.date_confidence: attested: 19 August 1946
stops.campa: In a frame house on South Hervey Street, his grandparents' house, a son is born to Virginia Blythe three months after her husband dies in a car wreck on a Missouri road. They name the boy for the father he never sees, William Jefferson Blythe III. His grandparents keep him until he is four. The town is called Hope, and he will spend a political lifetime saying the word as though it settled an argument. The house is restored as a national historic site while he is still alive to walk through it, and he walks through it.
suggested_refs: The William Jefferson Clinton Birthplace Home National Historic Site, South Hervey Street, Hope
sources: National Park Service, William J. Clinton Birthplace Home NHS

stops.name: Hot Springs, Arkansas: the borrowed surname
stops.date_confidence: the remarriage and the move are dated only to 1950; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Virginia marries Roger Clinton Sr., a car dealer with a drinking problem, and the family leaves Hope for the spa town in the Ouachitas. A brother, Roger Jr., is born in 1956. The boy takes his stepfather's surname at school years before he asks the law for it, and makes it legal at about fifteen. He passes through St. John's Catholic Elementary, Ramble Elementary, and Hot Springs High School, where he plays saxophone in a jazz trio. He leaves the Park Avenue house in 1964 with a surname borrowed from a difficult household and a practiced ease among strangers in a room.
suggested_refs: The Clinton house at 1011 Park Avenue, Hot Springs
Clinton, My Life (2004), on the Hot Springs years

stops.name: The White House Rose Garden: the Boys Nation handshake
stops.date_confidence: attested: 24 July 1963
stops.campa: Arkansas sends him to Washington as an American Legion Boys Nation delegate, seventeen years old and visibly already running for something. The delegates are lined up on the grass; President Kennedy comes down the row shaking hands, and the camera catches the boy from Hot Springs reaching first. Four months later Kennedy is dead. The photograph outlives him and becomes the founding image of a career, cut into every campaign film thereafter as the instant the vocation arrived. Clinton has told the story so often that its truth and its use can no longer be pulled apart.
suggested_refs: The Boys Nation handshake photograph, John F. Kennedy Presidential Library photo archive
sources: Miller Center, University of Virginia, 'Bill Clinton: Life Before the Presidency'

stops.name: Georgetown University: the School of Foreign Service and Fulbright's office
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month set to the start of the academic year, day defaulted
stops.campa: He enrolls in the School of Foreign Service and works part time in the office of Senator J. William Fulbright of Arkansas, chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee and the loudest Senate voice against the war in Vietnam. Clinton later names the senator as the formative mentor of his politics, the man who taught him that a great power can be wrong and can say so out loud. He takes his degree in foreign service in 1968 and applies at once for a scholarship that will carry him out of the country and out of reach of the war he is arguing about.
suggested_refs: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff records of the Fulbright chairmanship

segments.name: Oxford, the Draft Board, and Yale

stops.name: University College, Oxford: the Rhodes years
stops.date_confidence: the Rhodes Scholarship and the entry to University College are attested to 1968; month set to the Michaelmas term, day defaulted
stops.campa: He wins a Rhodes Scholarship and goes up to University College with the American war at his back, reading and traveling rather than finishing a degree. He crosses Europe and enters the Soviet Union, a trip his opponents will later comb through for treason and come away with nothing. He takes no degree at Oxford and states no public position on the war he is not fighting. He is twenty-two, and for two years he lives at exactly the distance from Arkansas at which a career can be planned and no vote can yet be lost.
suggested_refs: Rhodes Trust scholar records for the 1968 American class

stops.name: University of Arkansas, Fayetteville: the induction notice and the number 311
stops.date_confidence: the induction notice is dated April 1969 and reaches him at Oxford; day defaulted. The ROTC arrangement follows in July and August 1969, the lottery in December
stops.campa: The induction notice is written in April and reaches him at Oxford. He comes home to Arkansas and reaches an arrangement with Colonel Eugene Holmes of the university's ROTC program, which defers him; then he abandons the arrangement and returns to England. In December the lottery is drawn and he pulls 311, a number high enough that no one will ever come for him. The letter he wrote to Holmes surfaces in 1992 and is read aloud on television for weeks. Two facts sit side by side and are never reconciled: he was not conscripted, and he had arranged not to be.
stops.quote: Clinton's an unusually good liar. Unusually good.
stops.quote_source: Sen. Bob Kerrey, quoted in New York Magazine; publication date unresolved, reproduced in Wikiquote's sourced 'Quotes about Bill Clinton'
suggested_refs: The Clinton letter to Col. Eugene Holmes, December 1969, published in full during the 1992 campaign
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bill Clinton', early life and draft section

stops.name: Yale Law School: the library, and Hillary Rodham
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the year rests on the couple's own repeated account; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He enters the law school in 1970, and in the library the following year he meets Hillary Rodham. The account of who crossed the room and who spoke first is the couple's own, retold in memoirs and campaign literature until it has taken on the finish of scripture. They take a degree apiece in 1973. What begins in that room is not a marriage only. Every office either of them holds over the next fifty years is campaigned for by both of them and attacked as belonging to both of them.
suggested_refs: Yale Law School class records, 1973

stops.name: University of Arkansas, Fayetteville: the first race, lost
stops.date_confidence: attested: the general election of 5 November 1974
stops.campa: He teaches law in Fayetteville and runs at twenty-eight for the third district seat in Congress against the Republican incumbent John Paul Hammerschmidt. He loses, and loses closely enough that Arkansas learns his name in a single autumn. Two years later the state elects him attorney general. He arrives too young, is beaten, and turns the beating into the next office, and no defeat in Arkansas ever costs him more than the time it takes to run again.
suggested_refs: Arkansas third district returns, November 1974

stops.name: Fayetteville: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested: 11 October 1975; Britannica gives the year, History.com the full date and the place
stops.campa: They marry in Fayetteville on the eleventh of October, a year after the lost congressional race and two years out of law school. She has followed him to a state that is not hers, into a politics that is entirely his, and she arrives with a legal career already running ahead of his own. Chelsea Victoria is born in Little Rock in February 1980. For the next quarter century every office he wins is contested in part as a referendum on the two of them, and the sources that praise the partnership and the sources that resent it never once agree about her.
suggested_refs: Marriage records, Washington County, Arkansas, October 1975

stops.name: Arkansas Governor's Mansion, Little Rock: the youngest governor in the nation
stops.date_confidence: he takes office in January 1979 after the 1978 election; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Attorney general at thirty, governor at thirty-two, the youngest in the country. He moves into the mansion on Center Street with a wife who keeps her own name and a program of road taxes and school reform that the state has not asked for. The house is a governor's house of the old Southern kind, columned and staffed and small, and he will occupy it longer than any other single address of his life. Nothing in it prepares him for how quickly Arkansas can take the office back.
suggested_refs: The Arkansas Governor's Mansion, 1800 Center Street, Little Rock

stops.name: Little Rock: the defeat of 1980
stops.date_confidence: attested: the general election of 4 November 1980
stops.campa: Arkansas turns him out after one term for the Republican Frank White, and the youngest governor in the nation becomes, at thirty-four, the youngest former governor. Chelsea is nine months old. He spends two years apologizing on television, in person, and in a paid advertisement, saying plainly that the car tax and the hurry were his own mistakes. The apology is not a private matter; it is a technique, and he will use it again on a far larger stage, with less of the audience persuaded.
suggested_refs: The 1980 Arkansas gubernatorial returns
Clinton's 1982 televised apology advertisement

stops.name: Arkansas Governor's Mansion, Little Rock: the long return
stops.date_confidence: he returns to office in January 1983 after the 1982 election; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He wins the mansion back in 1982 and holds it through the elections of 1984, 1986, and 1990, ten unbroken years in the same rooms. He chairs the National Governors Association in 1986 and the Democratic Leadership Council in 1990, building out of a poor state's governorship a national argument: that a Democrat can talk about work, welfare, and crime without borrowing the words from the other party. The country will meet that argument in 1992 as though it were new. Arkansas has been listening to it for a decade.
suggested_refs: National Governors Association chairmanship records, 1986
Democratic Leadership Council papers, 1990

stops.name: Hilton Head Island, South Carolina: Renaissance Weekend
stops.date_confidence: recurring rather than single: the sources give repeated New Year's attendance across the 1980s and 1990s, with no one year named; the date stands for the series
stops.campa: Every New Year for years the Clintons fly to the sea islands for Renaissance Weekend, the invitation-only retreat where lawyers, academics, journalists and their children argue in panels for four days and go home with each other's telephone numbers. Supporters describe a seminar. Critics describe a guest list. Both descriptions are accurate, and the second one is the one that survives into the coverage of everything he does afterward. The weekend later moves to Charleston; the reputation it built for him does not move anywhere.
suggested_refs: Renaissance Weekend programs, Hilton Head Island, 1980s and 1990s
sources: Contemporary press coverage of the Renaissance Weekend retreats

stops.name: The White House: the inauguration of the forty-second president
stops.date_confidence: attested: 20 January 1993
stops.campa: He is sworn in at forty-six, having taken 370 electoral votes in November against the incumbent George H. W. Bush and the independent Ross Perot. The Cold War is over, the incumbent won a war and lost an economy, and the man from Hope arrives at the address he first saw at seventeen from the wrong side of a rope line in the Rose Garden. The speech is about renewal and about the young. He is the first president born after the Second World War, and he is careful to say so.
stops.quote: There is nothing wrong with America that cannot be cured by what is right with America.
stops.quote_source: First Inaugural Address, Washington, D.C., 20 January 1993 (The American Presidency Project)
suggested_refs: The First Inaugural Address, 20 January 1993, full transcript
sources: The American Presidency Project, First Inaugural Address (presidency.ucsb.edu)

stops.name: The White House: the trade bill and the wave
stops.date_confidence: the NAFTA implementation legislation is signed in December 1993; day defaulted to 01. The midterm elections fall in November 1994
stops.campa: He signs the North American Free Trade Agreement into implementing law with Republican votes and against much of his own party, and eleven months later the Republicans take both houses of Congress for the first time in forty years. The rest of the presidency is conducted from inside that arithmetic: budget surpluses by the end of the decade, an opposition Congress for six of the eight years, and a governing style built out of borrowing the other side's positions before they can be used against him.
stops.quote: I think Bill Clinton was the best Republican president we've had in a while.
stops.quote_source: Alan Greenspan, NBC Meet the Press, 23 September 2007, reproduced in Wikiquote's sourced 'Quotes about Bill Clinton'
suggested_refs: The NAFTA Implementation Act, December 1993
Congressional Budget Office surplus figures for fiscal years 1998 to 2001

stops.name: The Western Wall, Jerusalem: the folded paper
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the sources give only the years 1994 and 1998, with no month or day; the earlier year is used and the date defaulted. The pin is the atlas canonical Temple Mount coordinate, not a separate survey of the Wall itself
stops.campa: On Middle East trips he goes down to the Wall, covers his head, and puts a folded paper into the joint between two stones in the manner the custom prescribes. The photographs circulate widely and the note itself is never read by anyone. He will spend eight years pressing for a settlement between Israelis and Palestinians and will leave office without one, and this gesture, a piece of paper pushed into a crack in a retaining wall, is the part of that labor that lasts longest in pictures.
suggested_refs: Wire service photographs of Clinton at the Western Wall, 1990s
sources: Contemporary AP and Reuters photo captions

stops.name: Royal Palace of Naples: the G7 of 1994
stops.date_confidence: attested: 8 July 1994
stops.campa: The twentieth G7 meets in the Bourbon palace on the bay, hosted by Silvio Berlusconi two months into his first government, with Kohl, Mitterrand, Major and, as guest, Boris Yeltsin at the table. Clinton is eighteen months into his term and the newest arrival is the Italian, a television proprietor who has been prime minister for eight weeks. Both men sit at this table years before either has any reason to explain his connection to a financier named Jeffrey Epstein.
suggested_refs: Communique of the 20th G7 summit, Naples, July 1994

stops.name: Brandenburg Gate, Berlin: the last Allied garrison leaves
stops.date_confidence: attested: 12 July 1994
stops.campa: Five weeks after standing at Omaha Beach for the fiftieth anniversary of the landings, he speaks at the Gate as the Allied garrisons withdraw from Berlin, five years after the wall came down. He invokes Kennedy in the divided city of 1963, which is also the summer of the Rose Garden handshake, and tells the crowd that Berlin is free. The Kremlin summits with Yeltsin over NATO expansion and nuclear reductions run in parallel through the same years, personally warm and strategically bitter, and nothing said at this Gate makes them easier.
suggested_refs: Clinton's Brandenburg Gate address, 12 July 1994, Clinton Presidential Library speech archive

stops.name: Oklahoma City: the time of healing
stops.date_confidence: attested: 23 April 1995. The service was held at the state fairgrounds arena, not at the bombed building; the pin follows the arena
stops.campa: Four days after a truck bomb takes down the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building and kills a hundred and sixty-eight people, he speaks at the memorial service across town at the fairgrounds arena. He is at the lowest point of his presidency, a president whose relevance has been questioned aloud by reporters, and he stands in front of a state's dead and finds the register the office requires. His approval rises from that hour and does not fall back. The bombing reshapes the tone of everything he says afterward about anger in American politics.
suggested_refs: The 'Time of Healing' prayer service, Oklahoma State Fair Arena, 23 April 1995

stops.name: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Dayton: the talks that end the Bosnian war
stops.date_confidence: November 1995; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The presidents of Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia are flown to an Ohio air base, housed in officers' quarters within walking distance of each other, and kept there under American mediation until they sign. The Dayton Agreement ends a war of three and a half years and freezes its map in place. Two years later he goes to Sarajevo to stand among the American troops enforcing it. The peace holds; the country it produces is a constitutional machine so intricate that its own architects describe it as temporary, and it is still standing thirty years on.
suggested_refs: The General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, initialed at Dayton, November 1995

segments.name: The Second Term: the World and the Room

stops.name: The White House: the welfare bill and the medal for Maurice Sendak
stops.date_confidence: attested: 29 September 1996 for the medal. The Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act is signed in August 1996; no day is given in the sources used here
stops.campa: In August he signs the welfare act, ending the federal entitlement his own party built, and two members of his administration resign over it. In September he hangs the National Medal of Arts on Maurice Sendak, cited for American illustration and children's literature, and in November he beats Bob Dole. Both ceremonies happen in the same house within six weeks. The man who drew the place where the wild things are and the president who signed away Aid to Families with Dependent Children stand together for the photograph.
suggested_refs: National Medal of Arts citation for Maurice Sendak, 1996
The Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, August 1996

stops.name: The Roosevelt Room: that woman, Miss Lewinsky
stops.date_confidence: attested: 26 January 1998, 10:37 a.m., Roosevelt Room, remarks on the After-School Child Care Initiative
stops.campa: Six days after the story breaks he holds an event on after-school child care, and at the end of it he turns to the cameras, points a finger, and denies the affair in eleven words that are replayed for the rest of his life. He is lying. He admits as much in August. The denial is delivered inside a routine policy announcement, in a small room off the Oval Office named for a president who liked the strenuous life, and the transcript files it under child care, where the archive keeps it still.
stops.quote: I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky. I never told anybody to lie, not a single time-never. These allegations are false.
stops.quote_source: Remarks on the After-School Child Care Initiative, Roosevelt Room, the White House, 26 January 1998 (The American Presidency Project)
suggested_refs: The American Presidency Project transcript, 'Remarks on the After-School Child Care Initiative,' 26 January 1998

stops.name: Kigali: the apology from the tarmac
stops.date_confidence: attested: 25 March 1998
stops.campa: The aircraft lands at Kigali and he speaks at the airport without entering the city, to survivors brought out to meet him. He tells them that the international community, and he does not exempt his own government, did not act quickly enough to stop the killing four years before, and did not call it by its name. Three months of it had taken some eight hundred thousand lives. He calls the failure one of the great regrets of his presidency and will keep calling it that for thirty years. The engines are running the whole time.
suggested_refs: Text of the Kigali airport remarks, 25 March 1998, Clinton Presidential Library

stops.name: Robben Island: the cell, with Mandela
stops.date_confidence: attested: 27 March 1998
stops.campa: Two days after Kigali he crosses the cold water off Cape Town with Nelson Mandela and is shown the cell where Mandela spent eighteen of his twenty-seven years, and the lime quarry that ruined his eyes. Mandela has been president for four years and will leave the office voluntarily in one more. The visit is part of a state call that also takes Clinton to Cape Town and Johannesburg. He is the guest of a man who has done the thing his own country has never asked of a president, and the photographers keep both faces inside one frame.
suggested_refs: Robben Island Museum, cell block B, cell 5

stops.name: Goree Island: the door of no return
stops.date_confidence: attested: 2 April 1998
stops.campa: On the last leg of the longest African journey any sitting American president has made, he walks through the slave house on the island off Dakar and stands in the doorway that opens onto open water. He speaks about the trade that carried people out through that frame and about the American republic that was built with them. Historians argue about how many were actually shipped from this particular house; nobody argues about what the doorway is for. He stops short of a formal apology, and the omission is noticed in every account written that week.
suggested_refs: The Maison des Esclaves, Goree Island, and its Door of No Return

stops.name: Great Hall of the People, Beijing: the uncensored hour
stops.date_confidence: June 1998; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He stands beside Jiang Zemin at a joint press conference carried live and unedited across China, and the two presidents argue in front of the cameras about Tiananmen Square, about the men who were shot there nine years before, and about what a government owes the people it governs. Jiang defends the crackdown. Clinton says plainly that his host is on the wrong side of history. The broadcast is not cut. It is the single hour of the trip that is remembered, and Chinese television does not repeat the experiment.
suggested_refs: Transcript of the Clinton and Jiang Zemin joint press conference, Beijing, June 1998

stops.name: Washington, D.C.: the grand jury and the meaning of is
stops.date_confidence: attested: 17 August 1998 for the testimony. The sources used here do not fix the room, so the pin is the White House as the Washington anchor rather than a venue claim
stops.campa: He testifies to the grand jury for four hours and admits an improper relationship the same night on television. Under questioning about a prior sworn denial he takes the argument down to the verb, and the sentence that results becomes the most quoted line of his life after the denial itself. Lawyers have defended it as technically correct ever since. Everyone else has heard in it exactly what they expected to hear: a man who reads a question the way a lawyer reads a statute, standing in a room where that is the only defense left.
stops.quote: It depends on what the meaning of the word 'is' is. If the-if he-if 'is' means is and never has been, that is not-that is one thing. If it means there is none, that was a completely true statement.
stops.quote_source: Grand jury testimony, 17 August 1998, printed in S. Doc. 106-3, vol. III, Document Supplement Part A, U.S. Government Printing Office, 7 January 1999, p. 510
suggested_refs: S. Doc. 106-3, Volume III, Document Supplement Part A, 'William J. Clinton Statements'
sources: S. Doc. 106-3, vol. III, p. 510 (text confirmed via Wikipedia, 'Definition of is'; no government-hosted copy was reachable this session)

stops.name: Waterfront Hall, Belfast: after the Agreement
stops.date_confidence: attested: 3 September 1998
stops.campa: Three weeks after the grand jury he flies to Belfast and speaks at the Waterfront Hall, five months after the Good Friday Agreement and eleven weeks after the Omagh bomb. He had come here in 1995 to light the Christmas tree at the City Hall when the ceasefire was young and nobody would share a platform. Participants on both sides credit him with pressure applied at the right hours: the visa to Gerry Adams, the telephone calls at three in the morning, the American senator kept in the room. It is the foreign achievement least disputed by his enemies.
suggested_refs: Clinton's Waterfront Hall address, Belfast, 3 September 1998

segments.name: Impeachment, Camp David, and the Farewell

stops.name: The Capitol: impeached, and acquitted
stops.date_confidence: attested: 19 December 1998 for the House vote, 12 February 1999 for the Senate acquittal. The Capitol coordinate is a standard geocode, not taken from the source pool
stops.campa: The House impeaches him on perjury and obstruction of justice, the second president in the history of the republic to be impeached and the first since 1868. On the twelfth of February the Senate acquits him on both articles, neither of which comes near the sixty-seven votes conviction requires. He stays in the house at the other end of the avenue for two more years, with approval ratings higher than they were before the trial began. The country has decided something about him that the Congress could not make it unsay.
stops.quote: This guy's a scumbag. That's why I'm after him.
stops.quote_source: Rep. Dan Burton (R-IN), quoted in the Washington Post, 1998, reproduced in Wikiquote's sourced 'Quotes about Bill Clinton'
suggested_refs: Articles of impeachment, H. Res. 611, 19 December 1998
Senate impeachment trial record, February 1999

stops.name: Camp David: the summit that ends without a paper
stops.date_confidence: July 2000; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He shuts Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat into the Catoctin woods for a fortnight in the last summer of his presidency and tries to close a final settlement: borders, refugees, and Jerusalem. It ends with no agreement and no signed text, and the two delegations leave blaming each other and, in part, him. Within three months the second intifada is running. It is the largest thing he attempts and does not get, and the folded paper he once pushed into the Wall is the only piece of that effort still legible in a photograph.
suggested_refs: Records of the 2000 Camp David Summit, July 2000

stops.name: Presidential Palace, Hanoi: the first American president in a unified Vietnam
stops.date_confidence: November 2000; day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Thirty-one years after the induction notice reached him at Oxford, he lands in Hanoi, the first American president to visit a unified Vietnam and the first to come at all since the withdrawal in 1975. He is received at the French colonial palace in Ba Dinh, addresses students at the national university, and attends the excavation of an American pilot's remains in a rice paddy. He never wore the uniform of the war he ends up formally closing, and the men who did are still being lifted out of the ground he flies over.
suggested_refs: The Presidential Palace, Ba Dinh District, Hanoi
Clinton's address to students in Hanoi, November 2000

stops.name: The White House: the farewell, and a senator in the family
stops.date_confidence: attested: 18 January 2001 for the address; 3 January 2001 for Hillary Clinton's swearing in; 20 January 2001 for the end of the term
stops.campa: Hillary Clinton is sworn in as senator from New York on the third of January, seventeen days before her husband stops being president, so that for seventeen days a sitting president's wife sits in the Senate that had tried him two years earlier. He gives the farewell address on the eighteenth, records twenty-two million jobs and the longest expansion in the country's history, and hands the office to the son of the man he took it from. He leaves at fifty-four, younger than most presidents are when they arrive.
stops.quote: But there is no title I will wear more proudly than that of citizen.
stops.quote_source: Farewell Address to the Nation, 18 January 2001 (The American Presidency Project)
suggested_refs: Farewell Address to the Nation, 18 January 2001, full transcript
sources: The American Presidency Project, Farewell Address to the Nation

segments.name: Chappaqua, Harlem, and the Logged Aircraft

stops.name: Chappaqua, New York: the house bought for a residency
stops.date_confidence: year attested: the purchase is made in 1999; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In 1999, while he is still president and still under judgment, they buy a house in a Westchester hamlet for one point seven million dollars, because a Senate seat in New York requires a New York address. It is the first house of his adult life that comes with no office attached, and this one he keeps. It remains the family's primary home through everything that follows, an hour up the Hudson from the office he is about to open and twenty minutes from an airfield whose logs will be read aloud for decades.
suggested_refs: Westchester County property records, 1999

stops.name: Harlem, 55 West 125th Street: the foundation office
stops.date_confidence: year attested: the office opens in 2001; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The first plan is a tower on West 57th Street. The rent is reported, the criticism is immediate, and he takes an office on 125th Street instead, above a shopfront in Harlem, where the neighborhood turns out to applaud him into the building. From these rooms the foundation grows into global health and development work: AIDS drug pricing, climate programs, an operation that raises money from people whose names will be litigated for the next twenty years. The symbol chosen in 2001 outlasts most of the arguments about the money.
suggested_refs: The Clinton Foundation offices at 55 West 125th Street, Harlem

stops.name: Dakar: the September flight
stops.date_confidence: September 2002 for the trip; the day follows the atlas Epstein file, whose own dating of the itinerary is flagged there as reported inconsistently across accounts
stops.campa: He crosses Africa in September 2002 for foundation work on AIDS, debt, and development, and for part of the itinerary the aircraft is Jeffrey Epstein's. The party includes Kevin Spacey and Chris Tucker. Senegal and Nigeria are on the public schedule; Morocco appears on it too, though which legs used which aircraft is not fully documented anywhere public. A magazine profile that autumn credits the trip with raising the financier's standing. Clinton's staff, foundation supporters, and the Secret Service are aboard throughout.
suggested_refs: Epstein flight logs, court exhibits in Giuffre v. Maxwell
New York Magazine profile of Jeffrey Epstein, 28 October 2002
sources: Wikipedia, 'Relationship of Bill Clinton and Jeffrey Epstein'

stops.name: East 71st Street, New York: Epstein's house
stops.date_confidence: attested: 28 October 2002 for the New York Magazine profile. The visits to the house and office are [R], dated only to 2002 by contemporaneous reporting
stops.campa: Reporting places him at the financier's Manhattan house and office on at least two occasions, each time with an aide and a security detail, and the profile that runs in New York Magazine that October is where the friendship first becomes public property. His name appears on at least seventeen flight legs in Epstein's records between 2001 and 2003; his spokesman counts four trips, one to Europe, one to Asia, two to Africa. Ghislaine Maxwell's name runs through the same logs. No document consulted puts her and Clinton in a room together.
suggested_refs: New York Magazine, 28 October 2002, profile of Jeffrey Epstein
The unsealed 2019 flight logs
sources: Wikipedia, 'Relationship of Bill Clinton and Jeffrey Epstein'

stops.name: 358 El Brillo Way, Palm Beach: the address in dispute
stops.date_confidence: disputed: no record dates a visit to this house. The date is a placeholder inside the 2001 to 2003 window in which the flight logs run, chosen only to hold travel order
stops.campa: Palm Beach recurs in the flight logs as a destination, and this oceanfront house six miles from the runway is where the town police open their investigation in 2005, an inquiry that runs into 2006 and produces a federal non-prosecution agreement in 2007 and 2008. Some published accounts put Clinton inside the house. His office states he was never there. No flight log and no court filing places him at the address as distinct from the airport, and the contradiction is recorded here rather than settled.
suggested_refs: Palm Beach Police Department investigative file, 2005 to 2006
Epstein flight logs, court exhibits
sources: Wikipedia, 'Relationship of Bill Clinton and Jeffrey Epstein'

stops.name: Little St. James, U.S. Virgin Islands: the island he says he never saw
stops.date_confidence: disputed: no flight log, deposition, or filing places him ashore. The date is a placeholder inside the 2001 to 2003 log window, not a claim of presence
stops.campa: The logs land at Cyril E. King on St. Thomas, two miles of water from the private island that journalism and litigation both describe as a place where children were abused. Nothing that has surfaced carries Clinton the last two miles: no log, no deposition, no filing. He has said repeatedly that he never went there and knew nothing of the crimes. Epstein himself, in a 2011 email made public, called the claim that Clinton had been on the island complete and utter fantasy. The gap between suspicion and proof is entered here as a gap.
stops.quote_source: Email attributed to Jeffrey Epstein, 2011, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Relationship of Bill Clinton and Jeffrey Epstein'; the characterization is Epstein's own and is not independently verified
suggested_refs: The unsealed Giuffre v. Maxwell exhibits, released in batches through 2024
sources: Flight logs and court exhibits, Giuffre v. Maxwell

stops.name: Columbia Presbyterian, New York: the quadruple bypass
stops.date_confidence: attested: 6 September 2004, Columbia Presbyterian Medical Center. The hospital coordinate is a standard geocode, not taken from the source pool
stops.campa: Multiple-vessel coronary artery disease is found and four arteries are bypassed at the Washington Heights hospital, three years and eight months after he leaves office. He is fifty-eight. The saxophone player from Hot Springs who campaigned on fast food and slept four hours a night becomes, from this table onward, a thin man on a plant-based diet who talks about his heart in interviews. The memoir has been in bookshops for eleven weeks. The library on the Arkansas River opens in ten more.

stops.name: Little Rock: the presidential center on the Arkansas River
stops.date_confidence: attested: 18 November 2004 for the dedication
stops.campa: The library is dedicated on the river at the eastern end of downtown, a long glass box cantilevered toward the water, holding the records of eight years and the account of them he prefers. His memoir, My Life, has been published by Knopf that June and runs to nearly a thousand pages. Both are the same instrument in different materials: a man who has been written about by his enemies for thirty years, writing the file himself, in a state he governed for ten years and left at forty-six.

stops.name: Pyongyang: one day, two journalists
stops.date_confidence: attested: 4 August 2009
stops.campa: He flies into Pyongyang as a private citizen, not as an envoy of the government his wife is at that moment serving as secretary of state, and spends a single day negotiating the release of two American journalists, Laura Ling and Euna Lee, held under twelve-year sentences. He meets Kim Jong Il, sits for the photograph the regime wants, and leaves the same day with the two women on the aircraft. The photograph is the price. He pays it without visible argument and does not discuss the visit at length afterward.

stops.name: Port-au-Prince: the special envoy
stops.date_confidence: year attested: repeated visits across 2010 after the January earthquake; no single date
stops.campa: Appointed United Nations Special Envoy to Haiti in 2009, he is in place when the earthquake takes the capital in January 2010, and he returns again and again through that year, co-chairing the reconstruction commission and, with George H. W. Bush, the fund the two former presidents raise together. Billions are pledged. Haitian critics describe an outsider commission deciding a country's rebuilding, and the record of what was pledged against what was built is contested to this day and is not settled here.

stops.name: National Portrait Gallery, Washington: the shadow in the canvas
stops.date_confidence: the disclosure is dated to 2015; month follows the Philadelphia Magazine interview, day defaulted to 01. The painting itself is earlier. The gallery coordinate is a standard geocode
stops.campa: Nelson Shanks, who painted him for the Smithsonian, tells a magazine in 2015 that he worked into the canvas the shadow of a dress on a mannequin, an allusion to Monica Lewinsky that hung on a public wall for years before anyone was told it was there. The official White House portrait is a different painting by a different artist, Simmie Knox, the first Black artist to paint a president's official portrait, unveiled in 2004. Two canvases, two verdicts, hanging in two buildings a mile and a half apart.

stops.name: Washington National Cathedral: the funeral of George H. W. Bush
stops.date_confidence: attested: 5 December 2018
stops.campa: He sits in the front row at the state funeral of the man he took the presidency from in 1992 and worked beside for the twenty years after, on Haiti and on the tsunami, in a friendship the older man's family describes without irony as filial. George W. Bush, whose own library dedication in 2013 Clinton attended on the platform with him, delivers the eulogy for his father and breaks down at the end of it. The pew holds every living president, and Clinton has sat in rows like it before.

stops.name: Clinton Presidential Park, Little Rock: the ground set aside
stops.date_confidence: no date: the subject is living. 2026 stands for the present and is not an event
stops.campa: He is alive, and this journey therefore has no tomb, no funerary monument, and no death date. What exists is an area in the park beside the library where he could be buried if he chooses, a possibility recorded in the descriptions of the grounds with no decision announced by him or by the foundation. The unsealed court documents keep arriving in batches, most recently in 2024, and the flight logs are reposted each time. The ground waits at the end of the glass building. Nobody has said whether it will be used.
